Looking into the results there is not much of a connection to the nuclear disaster of
Fukushima. The slight increase in the radioactivity category occurred because of the
pictures of applications like cancer treatment that were linked to nuclear radiation.
Overall, the results correspond with the previous study and the overall trend in the
appearance of the different motifs, although there are some interesting exceptions, like
the picture of lasers from above.
decisions.reason: The paper directly compares its replication results against Neumann and Hopf (2013), ruling out 'descriptive only' (shipped). Setting aside the new within-sample town-versus-countryside comparison (RQ3, lines 450-473, 548-551) and exploratory etymology subcategory (RQ4, lines 442-448, 520-546), the authors' explicit comparisons to the original Neumann and Hopf (2013) findings are mixed rather than uniformly successful: (1) on RQ1 (overall motif frequencies across the five main categories, lines 366-380) and RQ2 (grade-level trends across grades 4-6, lines 396-416), the authors confirm the dominant sun motif (~70%), unchanged sun and radioactivity proportions compared to 2011, and a very similar grade-level trend ('Overall, the results correspond with the previous study and the overall trend in the appearance of the different motifs, although there are some interesting exceptions, like the picture of lasers from above', lines 497-499); (2) however, the authors also explicitly mark multiple original-specific contrasts, stating in the Abstract that 'a number of differences could be realized when compared to the reference study' (lines 32-35, with statistically significant increases in mobile phones [reversing the 2009-2011 decrease in the original], monitors, and artificial light sources, lines 370-379), reporting 13.7% positive connotations in radioactivity drawings and barely any association with Fukushima in contrast to Neumann and Hopf's finding of 81.4% negative connotations and only three positive drawings after Fukushima (lines 31-32, 434-440), and rejecting the hypothesis derived from Neumann and Hopf's Fukushima media-coverage explanation ('The initial hypotheses that the frequency of motifs related to radioactivity should decrease could not be confirmed. The increase in the initial study can therefore not be linked easily to the media coverage', lines 506-518); and (3) the authors summarize the replication in their final paragraph as having 'helped to solidify some results from the original study' (line 553). Under the codebook, because the authors present their evidence as confirming some original findings while explicitly contrasting others, the outcome is 'mixed'.
